jobs.title: Practice Professor or Associate Practice Professor
jobs.institution: Johns Hopkins University: Department of Health Policy and Management
jobs.description:
Faculty Search: Addiction Policy
The Department of Health Policy and Management (HPM) of the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health is searching for an exceptional individual with significant practical experience in addiction policy to join our faculty. This is a unique opportunity for someone who has made change happen at a local, state, or national level to join with researchers, other practitioners, students, and staff to address the crisis of addiction and overdose in the United States.
The role has two primary components.
Part 1: The Bloomberg Overdose Prevention Initiative. Approximately half of the selected faculty member’s time will be dedicated to this project, which aims to reduce overdose in selected states and, through informing policy, the entire nation. Multiple faculty members, staff, and students at the School are engaged in research, technical assistance and other activities, in coordination with teams at Pew Charitable Trusts, the CDC Foundation, and Vital Strategies. The selected faculty member will contribute to key elements of this work and serve as a resource to partner organizations.
Part 2: The Bloomberg American Health Initiative. The faculty member will also be supported by endowment funding from this Initiative, now in its 10th year. The faculty member will teach in the Department of Health Policy and Management, advise students, participate in other Initiative activities including the annual Bloomberg American Health Summit, and pursue their own projects in the area of addiction and overdose. For more about the Bloomberg American Health Initiative, visit http://americanhealth.jhu.edu.
The Department of Health Policy and Management is a premier, policy-centered academic department with faculty, students, and staff committed to solving the most entrenched public health challenges in the world through evidence-based policy change. Consistently ranked #1 by U.S. News & World Report, HPM combines rigorous multidisciplinary research with comprehensive educational programs to prepare the next generation of healthcare leaders, policy analysts, and administrators. The selected faculty member will be an active member of the Department, able to engage with faculty, students, and staff, as well as Centers, such as the Center for Mental Health and Addiction Policy.
The selected faculty member will join the non-tenure track faculty at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health faculty at the rank of Practice Professor or Associate Practice Professor. For an appropriate candidate, an appointment to Distinguished Professor of the Practice may be considered.

jobs.description:
The Division of Otolaryngology at Stony Brook University Renaissance School of Medicine is seeking a qualified candidate for a one-year Advanced Otology Fellowship.
This non-ACGME fellowship offers comprehensive training in advanced otologic and neurotologic surgery, preparing the fellow for independent practice and a competitive academic or private practice career in otology. The fellow will be appointed at the rank of Clinical Instructor.
The fellowship provides extensive surgical experience, including tympanoplasty, canal wall up and canal wall down mastoidectomy, stapes surgery, ossicular reconstruction, cochlear implantation, facial nerve decompression, lateral temporal bone resection, superior canal dehiscence repair, and cerebellopontine angle tumor surgery. Graduated autonomy is emphasized, with appropriate faculty supervision.
The fellow will run two outpatient clinics weekly, participate in an attending-level call schedule, and manage a diverse otolaryngology patient population with a strong emphasis on otologic disease. Unlimited access to the temporal bone laboratory is provided, and the fellow will play an active role in resident education and temporal bone dissection teaching.
Research and scholarly activity are strongly encouraged, with opportunities to publish and present at national and international meetings, including the American Otologic Society and American Neurotologic Society.

jobs.title: Forensic Science Associate/Full Professor
jobs.institution: Arizona State University: School of Interdisciplinary Forensics
jobs.description:
The School of Interdisciplinary Forensics (SIF) in the New College of Interdisciplinary Arts and Sciences (New College) at Arizona State University (ASU) invites applications for one full-time, benefits-eligible tenured faculty position in the forensic science program at the rank of Associate or Full Professor. Salary and rank are based on qualifications at hire. The anticipated start date is August 2027.
The area of specialization is open. Preference will be given to candidates whose expertise is not currently represented or is underrepresented among SIF faculty, or whose work contributes to a growth area such as humanitarian forensics, wildlife forensics, or forensic pathology. We are particularly interested in candidates whose research incorporates artificial intelligence, machine learning, or data visualization in ways that help bridge forensic science and digital forensics, although such expertise is preferred rather than required.
About the School:
SIF bridges science, law, and justice, offering a unique approach to forensic research and education. The School has strengths in the psychological sciences (including social, clinical, and developmental psychology, as well as psychology and law), the natural sciences (including anthropology, biology, chemistry, entomology, and genetics), and information technology (including cybersecurity and digital forensics). We integrate a wide array of disciplines, providing students with a comprehensive understanding of the role of science and technology in the legal system. With a focus on real-world applications and ethical considerations, SIF prepares students for careers that require scientific and technical expertise and a commitment to improving the administration of justice.
Our forensic science programs include courses in core natural sciences, such as anatomy, anthropology, biology, chemistry, entomology, and toxicology, as well as in application of these sciences to the law and legal proceedings in specialized classes such as death investigations, advanced scene mapping, statistical applications in forensic science, fundamentals of forensic analysis, forensic anthropology, forensic botany, forensic chemistry, forensic molecular biology, forensic entomology, forensic photography, forensic toxicology, analysis of human and nonhuman DNA evidence, human osteology and forensic techniques, humanitarian forensics, wildlife forensics, and seminars in a variety of advanced forensic science topics. Accordingly, we encourage candidates with expertise in a broad array of forensic sciences and closely related fields to apply.

At ASU’s New College of Interdisciplinary Arts and Sciences, we take pride in breaking down disciplinary barriers, cultivating an environment where innovative research flourishes. Our faculty are not just educators; they are trailblazers in their fields, consistently expanding the frontiers of knowledge. We invite you to join this dynamic community, where you will lead and engage in pioneering projects that redefine academic excellence.
Our interdisciplinary approach offers you unparalleled opportunities for personal and professional growth. By joining our faculty, you’re not just advancing your career; you’re shaping the future of education and research in meaningful ways. You’ll be empowered to innovate and address complex global challenges, all while preparing the next generation of leaders. We are committed to supporting and guiding you throughout your academic journey, ensuring that your contributions are impactful and transformative. New College is located on ASU’s West Valley campus, blending a liberal arts and science education with 21st-century workforce preparation and a learning hub for students of all ages and backgrounds supporting the rapid growth of its surrounding 14 communities. Integrating modern amenities with the natural beauty of outdoor spaces, the West Valley campus offers over 125 undergraduate and graduate degree programs across business, engineering, education, and the New College of Interdisciplinary Arts and Sciences.
About Arizona State University:
Arizona State University, ranked the No. 1 “Most Innovative School” in the nation by U.S. News & World Report for twelve years in succession, has forged the model for a New American University. Year after year, ASU ranks at or near the top of the list in areas that matter. ASU is a comprehensive public research institution, measured not by whom it excludes, but by whom it includes and how they succeed; advancing research and discovery of public value; and assuming fundamental responsibility for the economic, social, cultural and overall health of the communities it serves. ASU operates on the principles that learning is a personal and original journey for each student; that they thrive on experience and that the process of discovery cannot be bound by traditional academic disciplines. Through innovation and a commitment to accessibility, ASU has drawn pioneering researchers to its faculty even as it expands opportunities for qualified students, attracting some of the highest- quality students from all 50 states and more than 130 nations. To learn more about ASU, visit http://www.asu.edu.

ASU is a comprehensive public research university, measured not by whom it excludes, but by whom it includes and how they succeed; advancing research and discovery of public value; and assuming fundamental responsibility for the economic, social, cultural and overall health of the communities it serves.
Successful candidates will demonstrate throughout their materials how their teaching, research, and service will contribute to the fulfillment of this charter.

Sustain a vigorous, nationally or internationally visible program of scientific research with forensic application.
Seek and secure external research funding appropriate to the candidate’s discipline and research program.
Create and teach undergraduate and graduate courses in relevant areas of forensic science in face-to-face, hybrid, and/or online formats.
Mentor undergraduate and graduate students in research and professional development.
Provide academic and intellectual leadership that strengthens SIF’s research, graduate education, and external partnerships.

jobs.title: Assistant Scientist
jobs.institution: University of Rochester: LLE-Laboratory for Laser Energ
jobs.description:
The Laboratory for Laser Energetics (LLE) is seeking candidates for the position of Assistant Scientist in the Omega Experiments Group to lead experiments in inertial confinement fusion (ICF) and related physics on OMEGA, OMEGA EP, NIF, and future laser facilities. Laser Direct Drive (LDD) implosions of DT cryogenic targets and focused physics experiments to establish a foundation for the pursuit of high-yield LDD using future broad bandwidth laser drivers, as well as nuclear, hydrodynamic, high-energy-density (HED) and magnetized plasma physics, are among the Omega Experiments Group’s key missions within the science-based Stockpile Stewardship Program (SSP) of the National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA). The successful candidate will perform research and development for the Omega Laser Facility and future, planned experimental facilities (e.g., the OMEGA-Next facility for ICF with broad bandwidth laser drivers, the Next-Generation HED facility). The research scope of this position encompasses the research, development, and use of x-ray and/or nuclear diagnostics to understand the behavior of extreme states of matter created on Omega for the ICF and HEDP research fields and to plan target physics experiments for future laser facilities under development at LLE. The position requires a candidate with expertise in x-ray and/or nuclear diagnostics who can lead technical, engineering, and scientific staff in the development, deployment, and use of novel ICF and HEDP diagnostics on Omega, and work with theoretical and computational experts to design target physics experiments and interpret the experimental results. The successful candidate will interact routinely with subject matter experts worldwide in ICF and HEDP research communities.
Essential Job Responsibilities
Lead ICF and related physics campaigns on the Omega Laser Facility and/or NIF
Develop advanced measurement techniques to diagnose ICF implosions and related experimental platforms using state-of-the-art x-ray or nuclear diagnostics
Collaborate with theoretical and computational experts to design ICF and HEDP target physics experiments and to achieve a physical understanding of experimental results
Collaborate with the world’s leading experts in HEDP and ICF research fields on the Omega Laser Facility and NIF by defining x-ray and nuclear diagnostic configurations, collecting experimental data, and interpreting the experimental results
Perform research and development for the future, planned experimental facilities at LLE (e.g., OMEGA-Next facility) and the NNSA complex

The Baslan Lab at the Department of Biomedical Sciences, the University of Pennsylvania (Penn) is recruiting Postdoctoral Fellows (computational & experimental), 5 positions in total, to join our multidisciplinary team of investigators. Our work focuses on studying cancer genomes, with a specific attention to the genetics and biology of a cryptic class of cancer associated mutations termed Copy Number Alterations (CNAs). These somatic events change the number and composition of chromosomes in cancer cells to yield cancer and immune biology that is almost entirely unknown.
To dissect these events, we employ a systems biology, top-down approach where advanced analytics of large datasets are coupled to focused perturbations (ex: shRNA, CRISPR, cDNA screens) in experimental model systems (e.g. organoid & cell line models). We also apply a bottom-up approach where we employ cutting edge methods to dissect novel model systems we develop (ex: mouse models).
Some of the techniques our group develops and applies are:
- advanced sequencing technologies, at single cell and bulk levels, to generate large multi-modal datasets.
- novel algorithms & computational approaches, based on maths, statistics, & machine learning, to nominate novel cancer therapeutic targets.
- innovative, molecularly engineered model systems in in-vitro and in-vivo settings (e.g. mouse models)
- highly parallel perturbation approaches; CRISPR, shRNA, PROTACs, small molecules
We aim to advance:
- novel therapeutics; targeted as well as immunotherapies
- early diagnostic as well as prognostic tools
- novel technologies that can be leveraged to address outstanding biological questions
Disease areas of focus include, but are not limited to, acute leukemias, sarcomas, as well as breast and pancreatic cancers.
The training/mentorship opportunities are in the following areas (among others):
- Developing computational and chemical biology approaches to advance copy number informed precision therapies.
- Studying cancer-immune cell interactions during cancer initiation and progression using functional biology approaches &
advanced in-situ sequencing/data analytics.
- Developing machine learning approaches to advance novel prognostic and diagnostic methods in cancer.
- Dissecting cancer genome evolution using the first of their kind, somatic lineage tracing mouse models,
along with human data analysis.
- Developing single-cell as well as circulating tumor free DNA sequencing technologies.
- Designing and applying novel comparative oncogenomic algorithms to advance unifying principles of chromosomal biology in cancer.
Prospective trainees can expect the followings: Mentorship, Freedom, Resources, Exciting Science, & Fun.

The Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania seeks an accomplished and visionary scientific leader to serve as Chair of the Department of Genetics.

Articulate and execute a bold vision for the future of genetics and genomic medicine.
Recruit, mentor, and develop exceptional faculty and sustain a rigorous scientific community.
Advance research excellence from fundamental discovery through translational and precision medicine.
Strengthen education and training across graduate, medical, postdoctoral, and undergraduate programs.
Build interdisciplinary partnerships across Penn, CHOP, the Wistar Institute, and affiliated institutions.
Steward departmental resources and core facilities and expand philanthropic engagement and visibility.

Candidates must hold an MD, PhD, MD/PhD, or equivalent terminal degree and be eligible for appointment to the Standing Faculty at the rank of Associate Professor or Professor at the Perelman School of Medicine of the University of Pennsylvania. A collaborative leadership style, the ability to lead change and deliver measurable results, and experience with or aptitude for development and donor relations are essential.

2. Evaluate competing creative, audience, and business priorities using data, experimentation, and strategic judgment.

jobs.title: The Levitt Justice Lab S2027: Constitutional Moments
jobs.institution: Hamilton Fellowships - Levitt Center: Hamilton Fellowships - Levitt Center
jobs.description:
The Levitt Center invites students to apply to this Spring ‘27 Justice Lab “Constitutional Moments: Creating, Sustaining, and Changing How We Govern with Professors Frank Anechiarico, Ty Seidule, Heather Sullivan, and Benj Widiss.
As the United States enters its second 250 years with the oldest codified constitution in the world, is it time for another constitutional moment? Trust in the federal government sits at or near historic lows, and confidence in the electoral process itself has slipped alongside it. Meanwhile, a movement most people have never heard of is quietly approaching a constitutional threshold: twenty states have already passed applications for an Article V Convention of the States. Whether or not you think the constitutional order is in crisis, more people are asking foundational questions about it than at any point in a generation; Who gets to write the rules? Who gets to change them? And what happens when the answers stop feeling legitimate to the people governed by them?
This Justice Lab will give students the tools to think rigorously about those questions – not as abstractions, but as lived, contested, and repeatedly re-imagined processes, approached through historical, legal, comparative, and aesthetic lenses. Students will step into the shoes of the original framers to write the Constitution, then reconvene as a hypothetical Convention of the States to amend it. They will analyze constitutional law through landmark court cases and the doctrines that underpin them. They will study how other countries in the Americas have handled constitutional rupture and refounding. And they will trace how the founding moment itself has never stopped being rewritten, from the founding documents as rhetorical performances through two centuries of American fiction, poetry, and film that reclaim, contest, and re-stage it. Students will leave with a working command of constitutional design, argument, and interpretation: how constitutions get made, how they break, and how they get imaginatively remade.
Experiential learning for this Justice Lab will include two long form role playing games in COLEG/GOVT/HIST281. The Constitutional Convention of 1787 focuses on the most fundamental political and legal event in American history. Students in the game, playing the actual delegates to the Convention, gather in “Philadelphia” to write a new constitution for the United States. The second game creates a hypothetical “Convention of the States” to add amendments to the Constitution. Students will also have a required evening event in mid-April.
Required Courses:
GOVT-273W / PPOL-273W: Revolution and Re-Foundings in Latin America with Heather Sullivan (M/W 1:00 - 2:15PM)
Nearly all Latin American countries gained independence in the 1800s, but unlike in the United States, many of their constitutions from this period have been swept away. Revolutions and large-scale constitutional reforms occurred throughout the 20th century and into the 21st. Some of these constitutional reforms were seen as a way to address profound socioeconomic and racial inequalities in the region. Others have been a tool for concentrating executive power. Some were motivated by both currents. This class will explore the causes and effects of these constitutional re-foundings as well as the processes through which they occurred. This is a writing-intensive course.
COLEG-281 / GOVT-281 / HIST-281: Common Ground: A Laboratory for Civil Discourse with Ty Seidule (T/Th 10:30 - 11:45 AM)
From the beginning of the American experiment, political leaders and citizens have struggled over how to create a democracy, how to sustain it, how to operate it fairly, and even how to discuss it. Discourse has always been contested – and not always civilly. The course consists primarily of two complex roleplaying games to help us understand how America created its constitution and how we might change it. The first game, The Constitutional Convention of 1787: Constructing the American Republic places students in the actual roles of the founding fathers in Philadelphia. The next game is “Convention of the States: Toward a More Perfect Union?” In this scenario, the states have exercised Article V of the US Constitution, calling all the states together “for proposing Amendments.” Can we change the Constitution? We’ll try. This is a speaking intensive course.
GOV241: Survey of Constitutional Law with Frank Anechiarico (T/Th 1:00 - 2:15PM)
In this course, students will analyze constitutional doctrines through major cases. We will examine the function of the Supreme Court as an instrument of government and arbiter of public policy as well as core doctrines including judicial review, federalism, interstate commerce, due process and questions of individual rights.
Prerequisites for this course are waived for Justice Lab participants
LIT2XX: Reconstituting the Constitution with Benjamin Widiss (M/W 2:30 - 3:45PM)
This course explores the Constitutional “Moment” as an extended sociocultural formation in the decades just before and after the turn of the nineteenth century, and as a recurring American phenomenon thereafter. We will begin by analyzing the founding documents as rhetorical performances, reading the aspirations and anxieties they express in relation to those legible in contemporaneous literary texts. Then we’ll turn to political, literary, and cinematic works across subsequent American generations that reclaim or figuratively re-stage the founding moment even as they radically re-frame its stakes and stakeholders. Likely authors: A. Hamilton, T. Jefferson, W. Irving, H.D. Thoreau, F. Douglass, E.C. Stanton, W. Whitman, A. Lincoln, G. Stein, R. Ellison, G. Lucas, L.M. Miranda.

A department with deep roots in medical anthropology and faculty who currently hold competitive federal research grants from the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation, among other funders
